Consideration of the motion of Hon. W. T. White (Minister of Finance) for the House to go into Committee on Ways and Means, resumed from Friday, April 17.
Mr. 0. TURGEON (Gloucester):	Mr. Speaker, before making any criticism of the Budget Speech delivered by the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. White) on the 6th day of this month, I wish first of all to congratulate the minister on the sincere and honest way in which he made his exposition of the financial affairs of this country. After years of increasing surpluses and expansion of trade in this country the hon. minister was confronted with months of depression which brought about a decrease in trade and an increase in the public debt, and he is to be congratulated upon not resorting to mathematics to cover up the actual state of affairs. He frankly told the country that the public debt had increased by nearly $20,000,000 during the last fiscal year.
He told us that the fiscal year 1912-13 was characterized by the greatest expansion of trade the Dominion had ever known, and that the revenue in that year had been increased by $32,581,686.09-from $136,108,217.36 in 1911-12 to $168,689,903.45- and the minister reminded us that in that year he had a surplus of over $56,000,000 with which to meet capital and special expenditure. In the year 1911-12 he had been favoured with the great surplus of $37,000,000, and in the year 1913-14 he had a surplus of $36,500,000. The hon. minister admits that he has been favoured with the three largest surpluses in the financial history of Canada. The last six months of the year ended on the 31st of last month have not been so favourable, and for those

months he has had to show fast decreasing revenues. The hon. minister placed upon ' Hansard ' a tabular statement showing the revenue by months. Notwithstanding an increase during the first six months of the year, there was a decrease of $10,538,000 in 1913-14 as compared with the previous year. The hon. minister has shown that the year just ended gave a revenue of $168,000,000, but notwithstanding that there was an increase in the public debt of Canada of $19,000,000.
The hon. Minister of Finance has had in the past thirty-six months surpluses amounting to $129,500,000. That is a very large sum of money. It is enough to build the Georgian Bay canal which our departed friend the ex-Minister of Public Works (Mr. Monk) promised to the people. In the election of 1911 he told his constituents that work on the Georgian Bay canal project would be commenced the day after his party came to power. Three years have passed and the hon. Minister of Finance has had surpluses amounting to over $129,000,000 but the Government have not made a start on that great project, even if they have given it any consideration at all. I am sure that the delegation which interviewed the Minister of Public Works last Wednesday, and which was composed of men representative of the whole Dominion, found that the Georgian Bay canal had not only not been commenced but was very far from being commenced. The Minister of Public Works announced that the canal would be built only on condition that the commission recently appointed reported favourably on the commercial feasibility of the project. I can understand a Government referring the engineering side of a project to an engineer, but I cannot understand why a responsible Government put on the shoulders of a commission the responsibility of deciding as to the commercial value of any project. The hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Foster) told us six or eight months ago that this country was flooded with commissions. I d'o not know whether he did anything to prevent this new commission being appointed. In my opinion, there is absolutely no reason for its existence. The 'Government of this country should take the entire responsibility for deciding as to the commercial value of the Georgian Bay canal. I regret that the Minister of Public Works stated that if the commission recommended the construction of the canal, it would be built, and that if they condemned it, it would not be built. I cannot understand how a responsible minister of the Crown

can make such a statement. Speaking for myself, I -may say that even if the negative report of that commission is binding on the Government of the day, it will not he binding on the Liberal party. The Welland canal would be to the advantage of the United States as well as of Canada, and of the two countries the United States might perhaps reap the greater benefit. The Georgian Bay canal, however, is purely a Canadian project. It would carry not only the products of the Canadian West but of the western states of America. It would bring a considerable portion of American trade through Canadian channels and in that respect is just the opposite of the other route. As I said, the negative report of the commission will not be binding on the Liberal party.
The Minister of Finance was forced to announce to the House that during the last six months of the past fiscal year our revenue had decreased. It is probably unnecessary for me to point out that had it not been for the action of the United States, in giving us a free market for our lumber, our fish, and our cattle, the Minister of Finance would have had to announce a still greater decrease in revenue. If our prosperity in recent months has been greater in the East than it has been in the West, that is due to the fact that the American tariff has so favoured our fishermen, in giving them free access for their fish to the United States markets, that they have been able to obtain better prices than ever before in their lives, and with their increased prosperity they have been put in a position to enjoy more of the comforts of life, and to buy more imported goods, thus contributing to the revenue of the country. The opening up of the United States market to Canadian lumber has saved the lumber trade in New Brunswick, coming as it did when the British lumber market was stagnant. But this is not due to the Conservative Government or to the Minister of Finance; in fact, it was done in spite of them. Had it not been that the tariff in the United States was reduced on some of our great natural products, the Minister of Finance, instead of having to announce an increase in the net debt of $19,000,000, would have had to announce an increase of probably $24,000,000. And notwithstanding this increase in our net debt, there has been no very remarkable increase in the expenditure on useful public works. When the Conservatives attained office the National Transcontinental railway was almost completed, and only a few
million dollars remained to be expended on it.
I call your attention, Mr. Speaker, to the fact that a large portion	of
our revenue during the two years of the Conservative regime, has gone year after year in	expenditure on	the
militia, the expenditure on which has now reached the enormous	sum of
$11,000,000 per annum. And this, in spite of the fact that in 1909, when the Right Hon. R. L. Borden was leader of the Opposition, he criticised the expenditure of the then Minister of Militia, in the Liberal Government, because it had reached $6,000,000 a year. I cannot myself see the necessity of this huge expenditure on armament, considering that the only neighbours we have are the most peaceful people in the world, which is proven by the fact that we are now celebrating the end of a century of peace with them, and I hope preparing for the opening of another peaceful century. Personally, I have as great respect for my right hon. friend the Prime Minister as any member on his own side of the House, and for fear I might exaggerate his sentiments I quote his words, as reported in ' Hansard ' of March 29, 1909:
So that if you look at the amount expended on both military and naval defence, you find Canada pretty well up to the standard of all the great self-governing dominions of the empire. But, X would venture to submit that our expenditure has, to some extent, been appropriated to the wrong purpose. What is the object of our military expenditure? I know that my hon. friend the Minister of Militia and Defence (Sir Frederick Borden) has stated in the House that the military expenditure of this country is not larger than is necessary for the aid of the civil power. I would hardly think that an expenditure of $6,000,000 annually would be necessary for that purpose, and, while I am not prepared at the present moment to lay down any figure which would be a proper amount for the people of Canada to set apart for the purpose of defence, I do most unhesitatingly say that of the portion which the people of Canada should set aside for that purpose out of their public revenues, a very substantial portion, and, in my opinion, not less than one-half of the amount appropriated for defence, should be devoted for naval instead of military defence.
A few short years ago, the Prime Minister, when leading the Opposition, thought that $6,000,000 was too much to expend on the militia; he said that one-half of it would be enough and that the other half should be devoted to naval defence. But to-day, under his Government, the militia expenditure which was then $6,000,000 a year, has gone up to $10,000,000, and not one cent, of it goes towards naval defence for the

benefit of the empire, about which we heard tunity of pronouncing their so much last year.
During the fifteen years of Liberal administration, hundreds of thousands of settlers were brought into the Northwest, and these settlers, consuming the products of the East, contributed to the prosperity of the country as a whole. In 1896 the population of Canada was scarcely 5,000,000 people while in 1911 our population amounted to 7,200,000. In 1896 the net debt of Canada was $258,497,000, and in 1906, ten years after, under the Liberal administration, the net debt was only $267,042,000, an increase of $8,545,000 in ten years, notwithstanding that during that decade there' was the greatest prosperity and progress the country had ever seen. From 1906 to 1911 there was a period of great expansion and railway construction. There were subsidies to railways, throughout the length and breadth of the land, and there was the construction of the National Transcontinental railway to be provided for, and although the Liberal Government spent $146,000,000 on the National Transcontinental railway yet all the expense of railway construction generally and one-half the expenditure on the Transcontinental were paid out of the ordinary revenues of the country. Notwithstanding the heavy expenditures by the Liberal Government for great and useful public works, the increase in population had lifted the burden of debt ' from $52 per' head of the population in 1896, to only $45 per head of the population in 1911. Any unbiased man who studies the record of the Liberal party from 1896 to 1911, must admit that no country in the history of the wotM bad ever equalled the progress made by Canada during these years.
It was a prosperity of which we constantly heard, and the people were happy and contented at that time. Great as was that happiness and prosperity, when my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition, then the leader of the Government, attempted to enhance it, hon. gentlemen who were then in the Opposition rose on their seats and said: We are prosperous enough; leave well enough alone. Not only did they say that in this House, but they prevailed upon their friends to repeat the cry throughout the country. Well enough has been let alone, and one consequence is that the net debt of the country has increased to between $19,000,000 and $20,000,000. The people will not leave well enough alone when next they get an oppor-[Mr Turgeon. ]
opinion, but
they will do better for the country, as my right hon. friend the leader of the'opposition intended to do.
I wish to express my views upon the situation which confronts us to-day and upon tne future of the country. I will not attempt to make a dissertation upon the principles, theories and doctrines of protection and free trade. There are men better qualified to discuss these important questions in this House and in the country. My learned and scientific friend from Red Deer (Mr. Clark), whom we are all so well pleased to see back in his seat, gave us his views upon the position and aims of democracy at the beginning of this twentieth century in America and in Great Britain. We heard last week from my hon. friend from Rouv.ille (Mr. Lemieux), who expressed his opinions upon these topics. We heard the other night from my hon. friend from Westmorland (Mr. Emmerson), who also gave us his ideas on free trade, democratic institutions and the protection of the people against the privileged interests. Therefore it is not necessary for me to enter into a dissertation of that character.
We all know that the goal and ambition of all nations should be free trade with one another, not only because the principle is sound as a matter of economics, but more particularly because it is the principle which is most conducive to the moral elevation of the people inhabiting the different countries, makes for universal peace, friendly intercourse and brotherly feeling between nation and nation and benefits mankind generally. It must be remembered that free trade in its various forms has always appealed to the most thoughtful men of the great Christian naoions, and has found powerful advocacy on the part of those who have been known as the leaders of freedom-freedom for the masses of the people in the exercise of their mentality and religious principles. It is a doctrine which appeals to men and to nations in proportion to their moral standard, brotherly feelings, charitable inclinations and high ideals of civilization. This truth is strikingly exemplified at the beginning of this twentieth century by the fact that the greatest free trade nation today is also the most Christian of the world -the great British nation. If I wished to take man as a standard in order to illustrate the view which I am endeavouring to

put forward upon this subject, I would point to the great Napoleon, who proved himself to be not only an able general but a wise economist, and who devoted his energies in the intervals between his military campaigns to making treaties of commerce which were nothing else than offers of free trade to those powers which he regarded with a friendly eye. If in these efforts to establish free trade relations the great general of the time omitted England, it was because he did not want to make treaties or establish commercial relations with that nation. Napoleon hated England and his selfishness overcame his better feelings. You can judge men as nations and here you have that groat conqueror of modern times offering free trade to the nations he loved and erecting a protective wall against the one nation that he abhorred. Free trade is synonymous with generosity, brotherhood, humanity; protection.' means selfishness and egotism. That is the nature of the one principle and that is the nature of the other.
I admit that with the conditions that prevail in this country, that with the nations around us, either close to us or far away, and because we raise our revenue by indirect taxation, this country cannot have absolute free trade with the nation® of the world, but, nevertheless, it remains the duty of every Canadian, every member of the Government and every party in this country to see that free trade in its direct sense he extended more particularly to the masses of the people, whether on the farm or in the city, who devote their time and energies to the' production of those natural commodities which are necessary to keep body and soul together.
But we are told by hon. gentlemen opposite, and by some of the Tory papers which I have time to look at once in a while, that we are advocating free trade to-day, whereas, when we were in power, we did not advocate free trade. I say that from the day the Liberal party came into power in 1896 the leader of the late Government and his party showed their inclination to change the condition of things as rapidly as possible. Without spending any time over the individual items in the tariff which were changed, I will merely stay in a general way that it was reduced in a great many instances ©specially on many articles which are the necessities of the mass of
the people. The tariff was reduced to a considerable extent and especially with the object of extending to the mass of the people a great privilege which had been denied to them up to that time.
The one great effort of the Liberal party in the direction1 of 'free trade was the inauguration of the British preference of 25 per cent and which was increased during the following year to 33i per cent. Although our friends on the other side of the House wished to .make little of the British preference, I say that it has increased our commercial relations with the mother country and it has' also given to the workingmen of Great Britain' millions of dollars every year by way of additions to their income derived 'from the goods that we have purchased from them. Our friends on the other side of the House have been opposing the principle of the British preference. They claim a monopoly of loyalty but when you want to do something that will help the millions of workingmen of Great Britain, these hon. gentlemen rise up and object. They want to have free trade with Great Britain, but on the one condition that Great Britain shall put a tax on the workingman's food imported from other countries in order to allow our products to enter Great Britain free of duty and thus enjoy a preference in the British market. They want Great Britain to hamper the trade relations which she has established with other nation® and to restrict those influences of civilization which must impress themselves on every nation that has the privilege - of dealing with her. They tell us that when we were in power we did not do much to bring about the removal of customs duties. But there were obstacles in our way. While the right hon. leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) was in power he was willing to extend the principle of free trade as far as possible in the interest of the .masses. Yet everybody knows that he was handicapped by the fact that the markets of the republic to the south of us were closed against us. For instance, it would have been unwise to remove the duty on agricultural implements at that time, because the United States maintained prohibitive tariff duties. And so it was with many other things. But the right hon. gentleman looked forward, as had all Canadian statesmen up to that time, to the establishment of reciprocal trade relations between Canada and the

United States. And when the offer of reciprocity came from the United States, the right hon. gentleman accepted it. And I need not take up time to show that for all practical purposes the offer made by the United States to Canada was exactly that which that great leader of the Conservative party, Sir John Macdonald, had made to the United States, placing it upon our statute book' as a standing offer of reciprocity. And it is well known that just before his death Sir John Macdonald declared that while he had not been able to secure the opening of American markets for Canada, he hoped the time would soon come when that condition of affairs would be brought about. But before this offer from the United States came, my [DOT] right hon. friend (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) was justified in not humiliating Canada by taking steps towards reciprocity which our previous experience led us to believe would not be cordially received. Practical experience compelled the statesmen of the United States to see that they could not go on expanding while keeping their markets closed against the goods of other nations. And when the offer of reciprocity came, who will say that the leader of the Government of that day was not justified in accepting it? I ask any man in this House, Liberal or Conservative, if it is not strictly true to say that up to that time there was but one sentiment on that subject in Canada, and that was in favour of reciprocity. So the right hon. gentleman accepted that offer and asked the people of Canada to ratify it. It was not ratified. For one, I greatly regret the result of that appeal to the people. A mistake was made, not by the leader of the Government of that day, bat by the majority of the people of Canada. But I am confident that the people of Canada are prepared, at their first opportunity, to undo their mistake and to accept the offer made them of freer trade relations between this great country of ours, which soon should have a population of fifteen millions, and the great nation to the south of us.
The changes that have been 4 p.m. proposed, and that have been made, have brought about a different condition of affairs from that which existed under the late Government, and we cannot see the case in its true light if we do not change our point of view with the change of circumstances. The offer of reciprocity, if accepted, would have meant that our farmers would have had [Mr Turg-eon.]	.
free access to the markets of the United States with wheat, rye, oats, barley, and other grain. They would have had free access to that market for their horses and other live animals, for cheese, butter and other dairy products. There would have been reciprocal free trade also in fish and lumber. We have free fish and free lumber to-day by the action of the United States Congress, but the farmers of the West have not free wheat. Hon. gentlemen opposite may say: Wheat is reduced 10c. a bushel. But that 10c. a bushel is enough to shut the wheat out of that market. Had the farmers of Canada ah opportunity to sell free from that duty of 10c. a bushel, the difference would be all the difference between a profit and no profit. And the western farmers especially would be encouraged to carry on his farming with greater enterprise and vigour by reason of the profit which this 10c. a bushel would represent. And so with oats. There is a duty of 6c. a bushel on oats, and the removal of that duty would mean a profit and an encouragement to the Canadian grower. Under the reciprocity pact, the farmers of Ontario and Quebec would have had free access to the markets of the United States with butter and cheese as well as with milk and cream. To-day milk and cream are free, but there is a duty on butter of 2-}c. per lb., and the same with cheese. And what is the position for the implement manufacturer? Under the reciprocity pact there would have been a reduction in our duties of 2} per cent. Hon. members opposite are claiming great credit to this Government for having reduced the duties on certain agricultural implements by 5 per cent. But the Americans have taken off their duties on these goods, thus opening their markets to our manufacturers. Under reciprocity all the benefits secured would have gone to the farmers, but at present the one to benefit is to the manufacturer. The farmer to-day cannot buy agricultural implements free of duty, but the Canadian manufacturer can exploit free of duty the American markets with its hundred million of population. When I speak of the farmers, I include the farmers of the East as well as of the West. Although the farmers of the East do not cultivate their land to as large an extent as the farmers of the West do, they are progressing from year to year, but upon the prosperity of the western farmers largely depends the progress and development of the East. Our friends on the other side claim that they are giving a great

benefit to the farmers of the West by reducing by 5 per cent the duties upon mowers and two or three other implements used by the farmers of the prairies, but I would point out that the duties upon these articles would amount to only one-third of the tariff collected on the various other articles-rakes, spreaders, and so on-used by the western farmers. Intelligent Canadian farmers will not look upon this reduction as a benefit; they will look upon it with shame as coming from a Government which should have more generosity, but which has as its policy the protection of the manufacturer. For the last fifteen years the manufacturers of agricultural implements in this country have had the benefit of a drawback when they have exported their products; under the tariff which has existed in Canada they have been able to compete in the different markets of the world. In spite of a tariff of 15 or 20 per cent they have been able to compete with the United States; they have been able to compete with the manufacturers on the market of Australia and on the market of Great Britain. Yet they say that they cannot exist unless there is a wall between the farmers of western Canada and the people of the United States. I say it is high time that the people of Canada opened their eyes to the situation; it is time that hon. gentlemen of this House realized that the farmers of the West should have free wheat and free agricultural implements as well.
Our friends say that free wheat and free flour must go together and that we should not accept the offers made by the United States. I wish to draw your attention, Mr. Speaker, to the fact that under the patriotic administration of Woodrow Wilson the United States last year put into force a tariff to benefit the masses of the people; to benefit the farmer and the millions of workingmen in the cities. In doing this they left open to the other nations of the world an offer of reciprocity if those other nations would remove the duties. In the matter of wheat and flour they have said not to Canada only but to >any nation which has imposed a duty upon these products, that if they take such duties off, the United States will open its markets to them. Argentina, another farming country producing large quantities of wheat, lost no time in accepting that offer of the United States; in taking the duty off wheat and getting the benefit of the large market of the United States. In doing this Argentina has surely shown no lack of loyalty; nor would we show any lack of loyalty in accepting, for the benefit of the
western country, this offer which was made to the world at large. We produce 500,000,000 bushels of grain; the time is coming when Canada will produce over a billion bushels of grain and we will need larger markets for that enormous production. Is it not a wonder that there are in this House and in the country gentlemen who are so much concerned with private interests that they say: We should not trade with the United States; we want to preserve oar fiscal independence. How would the Canadian lose his fiscal independence by taking advantage of the offer made toy the United States? The Englishman is a businessman all over the world; 'he goes across every ocean and trades on every soil and in doing so he lacks no loyalty to Great Britain, and does not fail to recognize her greatness.
Our friends say: We will have to instruct the farmer and wait until he gets the benefit of our instruction. I am for instruction all the time in every branch of activity. Technical education has no stronger advocate than the modest member for Gloucester.
I hope-particularly after having read the report of Dr. Robertson on technical education-that some day Canada will have a realization of the necessity of education in every walk of life. Our friends say they will educate the people with the $1,000,000 a year given by the Minister of Agriculture, and the $12,000,000 given by the Minister of Militia for the purpose of teaching the children of the nation how to kill their neighbours. That is a great education for the farmer. We want education, but we want it in the right way, we want to have it exerted in the proper direction.
Our friends on the other side say:	If
you do not give protection to the manufacturer we will have destitute homes in our cities. I would like to ask the hon. member for North York (Mr. Armstrong) who made that statement if these agricultural implements are for the use of the workingman in the city? They aTe for the use of the farmers and the wider market the farmer has the more implements he will use. The way to benefit the manufacturer of agricultural implements is to open the markets of the world to the farmers. The farmer, having a larger market for his products, will then use more implements, and the manufacturer will reap the benefit. The rejection of reciprocity by the people two years ago resulted not only in the farmers of the West losing $20,000,000 upon their crop but in the manufacturer losing the benefit of the larger demand for implements

on the part of the farmer which would have resulted had reciprocity gone into effect. The manufacturers of Toronto, who are demanding a protective tariff and who do not want to see the markets of the United States opened to the western farmer, would have benefited by the increased demand for agricultural implements. And what loss would our country suffer by the free admission of flour? Our home market is, of course, necessary for the farmers; but we must also seek markets in other countries. If our producers were satisfied with the home market they would not have the opportunity for expansion of trade which is essential to their prosperity. It is the right and the duty of farmers and producers to seek an entrance to the markets of the world.
Hear, hear.

I am glad to be supported by the hon. member for Peterborough. He has both producers and manufacturers in his constituency, and he has intelligence and patriotism enough to appreciate and acknowledge the force of what I have said. Flour i3 used by every man, by the poor workingman just as by the rich man; and if you have any feeling or sympathy for the hard-working man in the cities, in the factories, on the railroads, in the ships which carry the product of farms to the market, the hard-working men of the eastern provinces as well as of the west, you should give them free flour. The farming section of the community must, of course, be looked after, but we must also care for the working men in the Targe cities. We know that during the year 1912-13 $10,000,000 has gone into the treasury of Canada from taxation upon food entering this country. If that $10,000,000 had been saved to the tax-payers of this country, if it had been left in the pockets of the people, more particularly those in the cities who toil for their daily bread, it would have been a great benefit to the masses of the people. It must be remembered that this tax on food is collected chiefly during the hard season, the winter, when Canada does not produce either eggs or vegetables. It presses hardest on the workingman, because he requires more on his table than the rich man, and it is generally the poor man who has the large family. The loss to the revenue need not stand in the way of this necessary reform. Piling up a large surplus is of no benefit to the country, as is [Mr Turgeon.]
illustrated by the record of the present Government. The Minister of Finance had surpluses for the first two years, but this year he adds $20,000,000 to the public debt, so that we are no better off than if we had not had the surpluses in the other years. Other countries not so great as Canada have seen the necessity of removing the duty from food products. The little colony of Newfoundland last year, moved by the same spirit that animates the Liberal party in this country to-day, in order to help their workingmen, in order to help their fishermen, took the duty off a great many articles of food which were most necessary to the fishermen of Newfoundland. They lost last year a revenue on these articles of $360,000, which is as much for that little colony, with a population about equal to that of the province of New Brunswick as $10,000,000 for the people of Canada. Nevertheless, last year the shortage of revenue has been only half that amount and the colony of Newfoundland has been able to close her fiscal year with a surplus of $115,000, equal, in proportion, to the great surpluses of our Finance Minister in Canada. I wish to read a brief despatch from St. John's, dated February 25:
In the assembly to-day the Finance Minister presented the colonial Budget, showing that the revenue for the fiscal year ended last June was $3,920,000, giving a surplus of $115,000, while for the current fiscal year duties totalling $380,000, having been removed last session from tea, sugar and salt beef, the customs revenue now shows a shortage of $130,000, or much less than expected.
What has taken place in the little colony of Newfoundland where the people have removed the duties from the necessities of their working men at the expense of a decrease in the general revenue is surely an example to us. The removal of- the duty on these foodstuffs has not produced a very serious decrease in the general revenue, and living has been made cheaper for the people of the island.
It has been said that wheat and flour are not in the same position because, in the proposed reciprocity agreement, a duty had been left on flour on account of a corresponding duty on coal in favour of the Maritime provinces; but to-day the same condition does not exist, as bituminous coal is admitted free to the United States market. Therefore it is said there is no necessity for us to consider that arrangement farther and that if the United States is willing to make our wheat and flour free, we should accept their offer in accordance with the-

persistent agitation of the farmers of the West. When I ask for free wheat, I, coming from the Maritime provinces, ask it because I know that it will be to the general interest of the country as well as to the particular interest of the provinces of the West. Our prosperity depends upon the prosperity of the West. Our harbours are enriched by the commerce of the West, and the greater the prosperity of the West the greater the prosperity of the eastern people.
Much has been said of the bounties on iron and steel. The Liberal party paid bounties on iron and steel during fifteen years, decreasing the amount on a sliding scale so that the bounties eventually ended in 1911. I admit that it may have been necessary to give such bounties during a certain length of time; and the period of great prosperity which we enjoyed under Liberal rule was probably an opportune time to give assistance to this great industry, particularly in view of our close proximity to the market of the United States.
I ask you, Mr. Speaker, whether this industry, which has been receiving aid from the people for about twenty-five vtars, is not now able to support itself? Sir John A. Macdonald when he introduced the National Policy said that protection was for the infant industries of this country, and it was his hope that after a certain number of years those industries would grow up and he able to take care of themselves. Suppose I brought a man of the age of thirty years to my scientific friend from Souris (Mr. Schaffner), who is always smiling in his wisdom, and said: This man has been nursed and protected for thirty years, but he cannot live without further protection. I am sure my hon. friend would be apt to class him as an incurable who ought to be sent to the state hospital. Why should our people be called upon to give further bounties and protection to industries that have created so many millionaires? What the producers of to-day want is larger markets rather than protection. Larger markets would enable the farmer to sell more, wear more and buy more. We on this side of the House are not the only ones who have been trying to get reciprocity agreements. My hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce made an agreement with the West Indies. We ail like to see trade agreements with British possessions, but the result of that agreement is not to be compared with the increase of trade that we should have had under the reciprocity agreement with the United States.
The Minister of Finance has taken it upon himself to give certain benefits to the importers of stone; he has reduced the duty on rough stone to five per cent. The hon. member for Westmorland (Mr. Emmerson) has already referred to that, and I just wish to corroborate what he has said. In my county, as well as in other parts of New Brunswick, there are large stone quarries having a market in Montreal and other Canadian cities. These quarrymen claim that the reduction of the duty on rough stone will be to the great disadvantage of the stone producers and even the stone cutters of Canada. They say it will benefit large building contractors but that it will not benefit the stone cutters because these contractors use stone cutting machinery doing away with the labour of the stone cutters. I, therefore, enter my - protest against changing the duty on stone.
I wish to say a few words about iron ore, which was the subject of debate in this House some time ago. The Minister of Finance in his budget gives no idea of what he intends to do. He says he is referring the matter to a commission under the Department of Mines. I do not think that a high tariff on steel or iron products would benefit to a great extent the iron ore producer in this country. In Bathurst we have a large iron ore deposit, perhaps the most extensive in Canada. It is considered of great value. The owners have spent a large amount of money in developing the property and have already installed a concentrator, to which I would like to direct the attention of the Minister of Finance if he were in his seat. Our importation of iron ore is small as compared with the amount of iron ore in Canada. It is true that the report of the Department of Mines for the year 1913 shows that a large amount of ore was imported, namely 1,942,325 tons valued at $3,877,824. It must be remembered that out of that 1,942,000 tons, 1,605,000 tons came from the Newfoundland mines, and was chiefly used by the Sydney people. It would perhaps benefit Newfoundland if she kept her ore and manufactured it within her own borders, but this ore comes to us from a British colony, which I hope will be part of Canada before many years have past, and so I do not consider it in the same light as foreign ore. Notwithstanding the many difficulties there are to-day in the way of Newfoundland joining Confederation, I firmly believe that not many years will elapse befcre the ancient colony will find it to hex own benefit, as it will be to the benefit of Canada and to the benefit of the British

Empire, to enter the Dominion. The Minister of Finance told us that Canadian ore was supposed to be inferior to ore obtained in the United States, but I call attention to the fact that the Bathurst iron ore is of the ve^y highest quality and is now being sent to the American market in increasing quantities every year, until last year the export to the United States amounted to 86,000 tons. I would point out to the Minister of Finance that the heads of the Mining Department, such as Dr. Haanel and others, are well aware of the quantity and quality of the ore from the Bathurst mine. I trust when the Minister of Finance appoints the commission of mining experts, he will see to it that that commission shall take measures to compare the quality of the Bathurst iron ore with that produced elsewhere. I would remind the Minister of Finance that the Canada Iron Ore Company has established at Bathurst a concentrator which has proved most beneficial, and the ore, after treatment, is now shipped to the Philadelphia market and is used in the manufacture of the most refined steel and iron products. That concentrator has cost the company $130,000, and the Bathurst ore is treated in this concentrator, so that only the pure ore is shipped to the American market, thus greatly lessening the cost of transportation. I would urge on the Finance Minister that if our iron ore industry is to be developed in this country, he should provide railway and shipping facilities, co that the cost of transportation may be reduced as much as possible. I ask permission, Mr. Speaker, to place on ' Hansard ' a description of the Bathurst concentrator, which would be of great benefit to the members of this commission, when they are looking into the question of the treatment of Canadian ore.

speechtext: The practice of placing on * Hansard ' extracts which have not been read is usually objected to, and without the unanimous consent of the House it cannot be permitted.
The other day the hon. member for North Essex (Mr. Wilcox) was allowed to print certain statements in ' Hansard ' without their being read, and nobody objected.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I remember some days ago that a request was made by an hon. member to place a number of tabulated statements on ' Hansard,' and when they were shown to me afterwards it was decided that they should not be printed.

Of course, without the unanimous consent of the House I cannot place the description of the concentrator on ' Hansard,' but I would mention that it is to be found in a publication of the Department of Mines entitled, ' Austin Brook Iron-bearing District, New Brunswick,' by Einar Lindemann, M.E.
In conclusion, after having reviewed the condition of Canada from 1896 to 1911, under the Liberal Administration, and having pointed out our position in this year, 1914, I say it is my firm belief that the policy advocated at the present time by the Liberal party is most conducive to the continuance of the prosperity which existed in the country before the Conservatives came into power. I assert with confidence that the policy of the Conservative Government offers no benefit to the masses of the people, to the farmers, or the workingmen, and it cannot, and will not, in my opinion, receive the endorsation of the people. I trust that before long the people of Canada will be given an opportunity to change their verdict of 1911, and if they should do so, I believe that a new era of prosperity will again dawn on this country.

I have listened carefully to the remarks of my hon. friend (Mr. Turgeon) who preceded me, but it appears that the issues he raised have so long since been settled by the people of Canada that it will be unnecessary for me to refer to them. My only excuse for taking part in this discussion is that I have the honour to represent a riding that is perhaps as deeply interested in agriculture of all kinds, in grain-growing, in stock-raising, and in manufactures, as is any constituency in the Dominion. Some phases of the changes which were made touched that fining, and they are already having their effect. But I have to remember that that riding is not all of the province of Ontario, and I have to ?o a step farther and remember that the East is not the West, neither is it all Canada, and neither is the West all Canada. Canada is a fairly hard country to govern, covering large distances from one ocean to the Jther, and with a sterile section between the East and the West. I take it that the duty of the Government is to do as much as they can for as many people as possible.
I have taken the trouble to look over some of the ' Hansards,' and I find that some of the gentlemen who have preceded me took the ground that the tariff was

practically the same under the Conservative party from 1879 to 1896 as it was under the Liberals from 1896 to 1911. I think they were correct, but there was such a very great difference between the conduct of the two parties that I must allude to it this afternoon. Some of us can remember the very serious depression previous to 1878, when there was a change of Government. We can remember that the Government elected in 1878 tried as far as possible to carry out the pledges that they had given in Opposition, and that the moment the telegraph wires were able to tell the story of the changes made in the tariff by Sir Leonard Tilley a new life sprang into the breasts of the people of Canada. I came into Parliament in 1887; I had the honour of sitting upon this side of the House then, and I heard the leaders of the Liberal party talking about that tariff during all the years that I was in Parliament previous to coming back in 1911. What was their course, what was their conduct? They decried it in every possible way. They told this House and the country that it was doing the people an injustice. So much did the people believe it that those engaged in manufacturing, and those with a certain, amount of wealth, were afraid to invest a dollar.
The Conservative party was defeated in 1896, and practically the same policy was continued from that day until 1911. We have been told that we had prosperous years during the reign of the Liberal party. I agree with the Liberals in saying that never perhaps in the history of Canada was there a greater period of prosperity. Why? It was because the Conservative party were loyal to their principles in Opposition as well as in power, and they stood at the back of the Liberal party when they were in power. Those who had money, those who had wealth, .manufacturers principally, invested their money without stint, which accounts to a great extent for the prosperity we had during those years.
I have listened with some interest to the story told about the farmers. I happen to be one myself, and I have some knowledge of what I am talking about. I take the ground that as farmers we have as much right as any other class in Canada to contribute a fair share of the taxes of the country, and when we are told that we should have free trade in agricultural implements and wheat, 1 say let us be
men enough to say that we are prepared to bear our fair share.
In regard to free wheat, it iB perhaps generally understood that we cannot have free wheat without free flour. I think we have arrived at a period in the history of Canada when we are likely to grow more wheat in the West in the years to come than we have in the years that are past, and the chances are that the price of wheat will go down. What we want in the West is a levelling up such as we have had in Ontario. I happened to receive a letter the other day from a western gentleman in which he says:
The crowd on the prairie that are shouting for * free wheat ' are a class of Americans who hardly knew Canada was a country until a few years ago. Constituted principally of men with local ideas, they seem totally unaware that the ultimate goal of Canada's wheat is Britain and that it is there the prices of Chicago and Minneapolis are set. If they were offered free wheat the probability is they would want an annexation rider attached to the agreement. As yet there lies before the leaders of Canadian thought the task of Canadianizing those people and this will not be accomplished by pampering to their local Ideas, or fostering their attachment to the country south of us.
The other day the hon. member for Assi-niboia (Mr. Turriff) trotted out a star witness. He impressed me with the idea that this man was wise in his day and generation. He stated that he had opposed the hon. member for Assiniboia during all the years they were together. That I could understand. The next point was that he was interested in an elevator, not in Canada, but across the line. Why did he want free wheat? Because he wanted to help the elevator in which he was interested. That was the star witness of the hon. member for Assiniboia.
I would like to refer to a statement made by the hon. Minister of Finance in his Budget Speech which appealed to me, and which appears to be the right position for the Canadian people to take. My hon. friend said:
We believe it to be the true policy for Canada and for every part of it if we are to regard as desirable stable business conditions and a deversified national life throughout the Dominion. It means the development of our natural resources, the maintenance and extension of our industries, a fair wage standard for our artisans and a stable and profitable home-market for our farmers, thus justifying its name as a national policy.
The hon. the junior member for Halifax (Mr. A. K. Maclean) in criticising the statement of my hon. friend the Minister of Finance, said that the farmers of the North-

west would have a good deal more purchasing power if they could sent their wheat in free to the United States. Grant, for the sake of argument, that that statement was true, where would they buy? Would they buy on the other side or would they buy in the eastern provinces? I have no hesitation in saying that they would form business alliances with the people to the south of us and would trade with them and make their purchases from them instead of from the East. It appears to me that if. there is one thing we want more than another, it is not reciprocity with the United States, but it is reciprocity between the different provinces of this country. What the farmers want more than anything else is that they shall control their own home market. If the manufacturers are in a position to pay their help a fair day's wage for a fair day's work and keep them at it all the time, that is very nearly all the protection that the farmer wants. If he controls his own market he has accomplished almost everything he may set out to do. I listened with a great deal of surprise to some of the statements which have been made in regard to agricultural implements. The point to my mind is this: are they to be made in Canada or shall they be made in the United States? I happen to live a short distance from a considerable manufacturing town in my own riding, the town of Oshawa.
After listening to these bon. gentlemen I have tried to reason it out in this way: would my farm and the other farms near that town be worth as much money if the Malleable Iron Works were done away with, if the Piano Works were removed, if the McLaughlin Works were closed, if the gas fitting establishments were taken away? If all this should happen, where would be our home market? It does appear to me that there is the answer to the whole argument in connection with agricultural implements-whether they shall be manufactured in' one place or the other. I am bound to confess that my observations ini the West leads me to believe that it will not make a great deal of difference whether they have free agricultural implements or not.
In this connection I believe that the hope of the West to-day is in mixed farming and not in growing grain. Why, to-day, it is reported they are sending hogs by thousands of dollars' worth to the East. That could not have been done a few years ago.
They are (Sending more to the United (States.

I was to going to make
(another statement in connection with the feeding of hogs, and I make that statement on the authority of a farmer who has been living in the West for a number of years and is engaged in hog raising. He says that at 7i cents per pound live weight for hogs, he can make oats worth 67 cents per bushel. Surely there is an opening for the people of the West, and it might be a means of using a portion of their wheat as well. The hope of the West, at any rate of many sections of it, so far as I can see, is in raising live stock to supply the shortages which at times arise in the East, thus affording a basis of reciprocity between the provinces. I do not look forward with hope to selling a great many horses in the West as we have been doing. But We will turn or twist in some way, striving iand hoping to be on top. I have said the hope of the West is in mixed farming; I say also the hope of the West is in better farming. I have always been- impressed in visiting the West at harvest time to see the difference in the crops upon the land which is properly cultivated and the crops upon the land which is not properly cultivated. They start with virgin soil and with land, perhaps, better than that of Ontario; but still the time must come, sooner or later, when something must be done to keep up the fertility of their soil, and in order to do this they will find it necessary to go into mixed farming. And with mixed farming they will avoid the mistake of having all their eggs in one basket.
The statement of the Finance Minister, it seems to me, reasonably meets

Looking to the future and trying to size up this country, I do not fail to realize that Canada and the United States lie side by side,-and parallel lines we are told, can never meet-and, speaking for myself and only for myself, I hope the day is far, far distant, when any foreign country shall dictate the tariff policy of this Dominion of Canada. Won't the same thing happen with wheat?

Let me explain that. The United States miller, I believe, does not want our wheat on any other conditions than those on which he gets it to-day. If the United States farmer buys wheat in Canada for purposes of milling and exporting, he gets a drawback of ninety-nine per cent on the flour exported; he is practically in just as good a position to-day as he would be under free wheat-but our farmer pays the duty. He says to the Canadian farmer: there is a tariff of ten cents a bushel on that product; you will have to take that much less. Take our cattle to-day; the large American packers are opposed to our cattle going into the United States; it is the smiali independent packer of Seattle, Tacoma and other western cities who are buying our hogs and cattle. In the same way if you let wheat, for consumption in the United States, go into that country duty free, the small independent grain buyer will come into Canada and buy grain, and you will get the best of the large American miller. The American millers will fight the United States president if he ever proposes to remove that duty. They do not want it removed: they are in a better position today because they have the ninety-nine per cent drawback. Many farmers in my own constituency are shipping their wheat, barley and flax to the United States market, paying duty, and making a handsome profit. If they can do that under the United States tariff, they could make a very much larger profit if they had free entry for their wheat into the United States market. That is why we want free access to the United States market, and I believe that the reason we do not get it from the United States Government is because of the opposition of the American millers.

-Many matters of great moment have been brought to-the attention of the country through the speech of the Finance Minister. The House will excuse me, therefore, if for a short time I refer to this particular matter. It is with regard to the item relating to No. 9 fence wire, which is under the present tariff admitted duty free. This No. 9 wire is used in the manufacture of ready-made wire fencing. Customs inspectors are furnished with what is known as a notch gauge, the width of the notch or opening for No. 9 size- being 144/1000 in. The opening for the -next smaller size, No. 10, is 128/1000 in., a difference of 16/1000 in. The wire that is found too large to pass into the No. 10 notch in the gauge is classified as the next size larger, which is No. 9, one of the duty free1 sizes. This permits of a great variation in the size of No. 9 wire, all of which passes customs duty free. A reduction of from 8 to 10 points in the size of the wire means a saving of from 8 to 10 per cent in the weight of material used, where this scant material is converted into

woven fencing and sold by the rod, which is the basis on which the farmer buys it. The opportunity for the maker of fencing to rob his customers arises out of his practice of buying goods by the pound and selling them by the rod. I have been in business too long not to know what has been done in this country with regard to the No. 9 gauge wire used in fencing. The practice with some makers is to order American No. 10 size, which is 135/1000 in., but duty free, as I explained before. The farmer has no means of gauging the size of the wire in his fence when he makes a purchase, and it is very difficult even for the trained eye to distinguish between No. 9 and 10 sizes. Let me illustrate the difference :
One lb. of wire, 144/1000 in. diameter stretches 17| ft.; 1 lb. of wire 135/1000 in. diameter stretches 204 ft. This extreme variation in the size of material used in the different kinds of fence, has made the fence question a confusing one for the farmer and he has been led to 'believe that he will get fully No. 9 gauge wire in his fence; and, without provision for testing after taking his material home, he believes that he 'has got what he paid for. Confinihg the size to be admitted, duty free, more closely to the standard of 144/1000 in. adopted by the Canadian Government in their specifications for the National Transcontinental railway, allowing a variation of not more than a few points below the standard, which has been done by this Government, should not work any hardship t-o the manufacturers of woven-wire fence, who desire to give their customers the size and measure of material which they advertise. This will undoubtedly benefit the farmer who to-day buys and pays for No. 9 gauge wire to be used in fencing. All we ask for in justice to the farmer, is that those manufacturers who advertise wire as No. 9 should be absolutely compelled to furnish exactly what they advertise. Advertising is conducted, in many instances, in a barefaced and bold manner in this country, and something should be done to curb this evil, which to-day has assumed large proportions. By this means money is being .-taken out of the pockets of the buying public, who, in my estimation, should be protected by some law governing advertising methods as is done in Germany.

Mr. Speaker, economic thinkers in the world to-day agree that the tariff is not responsible for the high cost of living, and

the theory that the abolition of customs tariff will lower prices and better the condition of the masses has been found wanting. Britain has had free trade for more than sixty years, and yet the cost of living in the United Kingdom is going up by leaps and bounds. Holland and Denmark are low tariff countries, yet they pay more for their food-stuffs than do the people of high protectionist countries like Germany and France. But, since Europe is far away, let us come nearer home. Why is it that the abolition of food duties under the Underwood tariff failed to lower the cost of living in the United States? Why, Sir, without going into details, the result has been that in the three months since the new trade policy has been in force, the cost of living in United States has not only not decreased, but has actually increased at as great a rate as during any equal period of time during the past ten or fifteen years. Some of the leading newspapers in the United States have been mercilessly exposing this policy, and they refer scornfully to the Canadian Liberals as opportunists.
Where will the free food come from when there is no cheap food outside Canada to buy? Living is high in all countries today. The National Policy aims to benefit the farmer and the workingman first; it benefited them by causing industries to be built up throughout the country, creating a demand for labour and a home market for the farmer. What do the people of the United States think about the tariff? I wish to read an article from the Iron Age, of April 16, 1914, entitled, ' Our Losses from Canada's Steel Tariff.' It is as follows:
We have already referred to the 50 per cent falling off in iron and steel exports from the United States, in the first two months of this year. While Canada's statistics of iron and steel imports in the two periods are not yet published, it is fair to assume that the business depression there, in the past year, is responsible for the poor showing in shipments from this side in recent months. Canada, as is well known, is the best customer of our steel industry.
It has been pointed out repeatedly that the preference granted Great Britain in the Canadian tariff amounts to little in comparison with the inducements to Canadians to do business with manufacturers in the United States. Canada's enormous steel trade with the United States might well quiet the fears of those who saw orders for European steel going out from this country as soon as a margin of, say, $1 a ton showed in the foreign manufacturer's favour under our new tariff. Canadian buyers of our steel have found out that it is worth more than one or two dollars a ton to be so close to their source of steel supply that shipments could be traced, that required deliveries could be met, that claims could be promptly adjusted, that the telegraph and telephone could give hourly contact with the producer, with mail connection a matter of over night. They have not underestimated, moreover, the advantage of the credit relations established with large manufacturers on this side of the line. It is these things that have kept Canada from placing more than about 10 per cent of her steel orders in Great Britain.
But what the preferential tariff could not do for British steel makers who coveted the Canadian market and have complained of the lack of loyalty that denied it to them, Canada is now to do for herself as fast as her steel manufacturers can get ready to benefit by the increased duties on iron and steel products. Only actual trade developments will permit of measuring the loss of trade the duties just announced will Inflict on American steel manufacturers. Our wire rod exports to Canada, which have been about 60,000 tons in each of the past two years, will be practically all cut off by the new duty of $3.50 a ton, as Canada's wire rod capacity is now ample to take care of the home demand. Wrought pipe shipments from this side will be cut down, particularly in the smaller sizes. It will probably be some time before any impression will be made upon the structural steel trade our mills have had there; but the Canadian duties on these products will be raised as capacity develops there to supply them. Such development is to be expected, as diversification of Canadian steel products will be forced by the decline in rail demand, for the great railroad building programme across the border is nearing the end. In a number of lines little loss will come to our Canadian trade for some years, though it is quite certain that the total of $120,900,000 worth of American iron and steel and machinery products shipped to Canada in the fiscal year

ended March 31, 1913, will long stand as a high record. Steel making has not yet been profitable to the larger Canadian companies; it will take years for the industry to become seasoned against such competition as may develop from this side, particularly in times of depression here. Mr. Speaker, my trade doctrine is moderate protection for our industries and a home market for the farmer, and I am willing to take up the gauntlet on this matter and fight it out to-morrow. We want and ask for no more favours from foreign countries than we are giving to them. Let us stand united as one people, filled with loyalty and enthusiasm towards our common country, Canada, which, under protection) has reached the point where it is the coming country of the twentieth century.

Some people say that the farmers of the West do not want to pay their fair share of taxation. That is an absurdity, and. more than that, it is a slander on the people of western Canada. If this Government proposes to legislate for certain sections of the country, then the sooner the sections that are to be left out in the cold become aware of that fact, the better it is for them. Here are the farmers of the West, men who have gone out as pioneers to break up the virgin soil, arid who have endured hardships and privations of all sorts, and, in many oases, hunger, and want, and cold. There are many of those settlers who have gone forty miles, fifty miles, yes one hundred miles, beyond any available railroad, hoping that some time in the future means of transportation would be provided for them. We find that after these men have gone through all this period of privation and hardship, there comes a time when they are able to hitch their team to a wagon, fill that wagon with the finest wheat grown in the world, and send it to market; but when they get that far, they find that the price they receive for the wheat barely pays for the cost of production. And yet, because there are a few buildings erected a few miles east of Winnipeg, with a certain amount of more or less valuable machinery in them, and because certain wealthy interests from the eastern part of Canada have come up there for the purpose of making money out of the milling of the farmers' wheat, the Minister of Finance says to the farmers: these men who have gone from the East and established their mills to mill your wheat, tell me that it will not be to your advantage to give you free access for your grain into the markets of the United States. True, Sir, these millers are few and the farmers are many in number, and the farmers have expressed, practically unanimously, their desire for free wheat, but the Minister of Finance and the Government bow to the wishes of the millers. Is it patriotic, is it conducive to patriotism, is it conducive to strengthening the bonds of empire that we hear so much about from imperialistic gentlemen like the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Cockshutt) and from other hon. gentlemen in this House, to compel our fellow countrymen to ship their oats and other cereals across the line and pay very liberally for the privilege

into the coffers of the United States? Take the item of flax, for instance. The Underwood Tariff, I understand, reduces the figures on flax to 20 cents per bushel. I mean of the late Government. I was not a member of that Government any more than the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Blain) is a member of this. I can imagine-though I have not been told-that the late Government put a duty on flax for the same reason that they removed the reciprocity clause from the tariff-in order that they might some day be in a position to make terms with the United States when the United States were willing to consider a reciprocity arrangement. I cannot see any other reason. But I think that the reciprocity agreement proposed in 1911 is the answer to the hon. gentleman's question. Because in that agreement it was proposed to remove absolutely the duty on flax and other cereals, and had that been carried out the western Canadian flax grower would be getting 20 cents per bushel or thereabouts more for his flax in the United States than he can get to-day. Of course, in relation to these items of flax, barley and oats, we have to put up with conditions as they are, because the Wilson-Underwood Tariff is not subject to this Government or the people of this country, it is a tariff made by the United States. But in regard to the item of wheat we are in a different situation, for there they still hold out the offer of reciprocity in wheat and wheat products. The
Minister of Finance, when he became a member of this Government attempted to make it plain to the people of this country that his duty would be to see to it that every interest in this country should be fairly treated and that he would do his best to see that the people were not oppressed and ill-treated by the trusts and wealthy interests of this country. How has he carried out that proposal? Why, free wheat, as he knows, means that the millers will have to pay the farmers a little more for their wheat while the consumers will get their flour at a great deal cheaper rate. Yet the Minister of Finance not only refused the requests of the western farmer for free wheat, but I believe that in this Tespect he has refused the request of his own followers in this House. So, you see, while the Minister of Finance is exceedingly sensitive towards the accusations levelled against him in this House and out of it, that he is a member of the Government representing a certain interest in this country, that he is, as it were, the hired man of certain interests, the position he takes on this question of free wheat, is to my mind absolutely conclusive evidence of the atttitude he holds towards the great mass of farmers not only of the West but of the East as well. For we must admit that it makes no difference whether a man farms east of the Great Lakes or west of the Great Lakes, there is a community of interest. I notice that in the province of Ontario to-day many of the farmers who were deceived and deluded into voting against the reciprocity agreement, are not averse to taking a higher price for their cattle and hogs which to-day they are shipping across the line into the markets of the United States. Under reciprocity?

I have under my hand an article published in the official organ of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, known as Industrial Canada. I shall not read the article, but it is headed ' Free Wheat.'
