In dealing with the question of the duty on agricultural implements I will be brief, because I had the privilege of touching on that subject in connection with the resolution introduced by the hon. member for Moosejaw (Mr. Knowles). As I understand it, the main object of a tariff is to give infant industries, as they are called, a chance to become established in the com-.munity where they rightfully belong, so that they can bear competition with similar industries in other countries.
In looking through ' Hansard ' of 1906-07 the other day in search of a reference, I came across a very excellent definition of protection made in a speech delivered during the Budget debate of that session by the member for Brantford (Mr. Cockshutt). Ever since I first read about the Halifax platform of the Conservative party in which they used the words ' adequate protection ' I had wondered just what was meant by that particular expression. I have' here a
definition given in the speech delivered by the hon. member. He said:
I do not claim to be a high protectionist, but I stand for adequate protection. I have sometimes been asked to define what I mean by adequate protection and I have replied that adequate protection is a protection that will protect. What I mean by that I explain in this way. If you ask me what clothes I am going to put on to-day, I ask you what kind of weather you are going to have and if you tell me I will know how to dress for it. If it is a cold day I will put on a heavy overcoat-; if it is a moderate day I will put on a light overcoat; and if it is a warm day I will go without an overcoat. So it is with the tariff.
That is the definition given by my hon. friend of adequate protection. If it is a cold day he will put on a heavy overcoat, if it is a moderate day he will put on a light overcoat and if it is a warm day he will go without any overcoat-and I suppose if it is a very warm day he will go in his shirt sleeves. That sounds like a very reasonable proposition. Would the hon. member for Brantford, having that definition in mind, tell us wl^en he considers it is going to be warm enough in this country to permit the Government to abolish the duties on agricultural implements? What kind of weather does he want? How* warm has it to be? Will it have to foe equator weather or, as my hon. friend behind me suggests, would we have to leave this world altogether to find weather warm enough to suit my hon. friend from Brantford. That I think, after all, is a rather fair illustration, if we are going to have a protective tariff at all, of what ought to be its object. The Minister of Finance told the member for Assiniboia the other day that if he,were consistent and were going to advocate the abolition of duties on agricultural implements, he must go further and pronounce himself in favour of absolute free trade. That does not follow, in my judgment. It absolutely does not follow the definition of my hon. friend for Brantford of the meaning of the term ' adequate protection.' Adequate protection simply means that you wear >an overcoat as long as you need an overcoat and just the minute the weather is warm enough so you can dispense with the overcoat you dispense with it. When does my hon. friend think it is going to be warm enough for the agricultural industry of the Dominion of Canada to go without an overcoat? The charge is laid at the door of hon. gentlemen on this side of the House that because we are

in favour of the abolition of the duty on agricultural implements we are in favour at the moment of the abolition of duties on everything else. I deny that accusation. Whatever my theories, whatever my principles of economics may be, I recognize that we must consider conditions as they exist in Canada to-day and govern ourselves accordingly. But does any gentleman in this House, in view of the fact that members on this side have moved for free agricultural implements, undertake to say that the agricultural implement industry is not in a totally different position from any other manufacturing industry in this country? Why have we a tariff wall around this country? To protect us, very largely, from importation from the United States without the corresponding privilege of exporting to that country. What has the Wilson-Underwood tariff done? Among the manufactured articles placed on the free list by that tariff are agricultural implements. They are absolutely free, so that whereas to-day the Canadian farmer, by what is practically an export duty, is prevented from selling his surplus wheat in the United States, he is also compelled to pay duty on the implements he uses, notwithstanding the fact that the people who manufacture these implements have not only the home market in Canada open to them, but the market of one hundred million people right alongside of the international boundary. Is that market of no advantage to the manufacturers of this country? My hon. friend for some years, I do not know for how long, sent very considerable shipments from his own factory across the international boundary and paid fifteen per cent duty, and a farmer near St. Paul could buy a plough a great deal cheaper than the Manitoba farmer, notwithstanding the fact that that plough had paid on it fifteen per cent duty to get across the international boundary line.
Who paid the duty in that case?

I care not who paid the
duty, that is an old friend, we have heard it often. The essential point is that the American farmer got the plough cheaper than the farmer in Canada after somebody had paid the duty on it. Whether it was my hon. friend or the interest who bought the plough from him makes no difference. My hon. friend was making a profit, and the people who sold the implement in the United States were making a profit, and fifteen per cent duty was paid into the

coffers of the United States Government, and yet the American farmer got the plough cheaper than the farmers of this country. My hon. friend must be congratulating himself on the removal of that fifteen per cent duty, because whether he gets a profit or not somebody must. He says it is a poor market. Is it a poor market? How then is it that the Massey-Harris Company or the controlling interest in that company went over two or three years ago into Batavia, New York, and purchased -a controlling interest in a large harvester work which they operate and control at the present time? If the manufacturers of agricultural implements in Canada to-day are at some disadvantage in reaching their ultimate market in western Canada on account of long freight hauls, what about the advantage they have acquired by getting free access into eastern United States for the products of their factory so that their products enter that market without one cent of duty? Some of these gentlemen say: You ought to solve this question if you put agricultural implements on the free list you ought also to put on the free list the raw material that enters into them. What have we on this side of the House to do with that question ? We are not the Government of the day. What we want the Government to do is to admit the principle that the farmers in Canada, in view of the fact that the United States have given free entry to the agricultural implements of this country, have borne long enough the burden of a customs duty on every implement they use on their farms. It is not our duty to say what shall be done in regard to the raw material. We on this side of the House do not want any manufacturing industry in this country injured. If it is an industry indigenous to this country we want it to flourish. Eight years ago the hon. member for Brantford boasted in that same speech that the agricultural implement industry of this country was in such a flourishing condition that even at that time they could compete in the open markets of the world. If they were able to do that then, surely after eight years of continued prosperity they can do it now. I do not attach so much importance to the question of free agricultural implements as I do to the question of free wheat. The Government have refused one proposition, we appeal to them to give us the other. They have given a five per cent reduction on mowers and binders, but all the operations of farming are not carried

on by means of these two implements alone. First of all, the ground has to be ploughed in the spring or in the fall. The Minister of Finance told us the other night that he had looked into the agricultural implement industry so far as binders and mowers are concerned. I wonder why he did not go a little farther in his investigation and consider the question of ploughs, cultivators, seeders, and other implements. I do not know that we have very far to go to find the reason, but whatever it be let me tell the minister that if all he is prepared to do is for the farmers of Ontario, of Quebec, of the Maritime provinces-I will put the farmers of the West last in this case-is to give a reduction of five per cent on binders and mowers, I am afraid that so far as any particular benefit is concerned-especially political benefit-my hon. friend might just as well have left the tariff as he found it.
There is just one other item to which I shall refer, and then I am through. Within the last few days-I presume my experience is similar to that of many other western members-I have received numerous letters and petitions from the different interests in my constituency, farming and otherwise, protesting against one particular tariff proposal, that is, the tariff on iron and steel products. I had looked into this subject a little before receiving these communications, and had come to the conclusion that if there is one indefensible feature in the Budget it i.s the proposal to place a tariff on wire rods entering this country. As the House knows, and as the Minister of Finance told us the other night, there are only two large iron and steels plants in this country manufacturing wire rods. These rods are the raw material for wire products, such as nails, screws, etc. The two companies are the Dominion Iron and Steel Company, and the Steel Company of Canada which is situated, I believe, at 'Hamilton. The Steel Company of Canada is a merger of a number of companies. I have some figures here which go to show that while the authorized capital of this company amounts to the sum of $35,000,000- $10,000,000 in bonds, $10,000,000 preferred stock and $15,000,000 common stock-the actual amount of capital of all the companies participating in that merger was only in the neighbourhood of $10,000,000- $10,000,000 real capital, $25,000,000 worth of watered stock, that is what it amounts to. No doubt the same is true of the Dominion Iron and Steel Company. That company has an enormous capitalization, somewhere
in the neighbourhood of $45,000,000. I do not wonder that these two great companies with their enormous capitalization and limited output find it necessary to come to the Parliament of Canada to have a tariff placed upon wire rods in order that they may pay a fair dividend on their common stock. The Minister of Finance explained the situation frankly and fully. He said that during the last fifty years small independent concerns had established themselves in -different parts of Canada, at Toronto, Hamilton, and other points for the manufacture of wire products from wire rods which were then free of duty. These independent companies were able to establish themselves because of the fact that the Dominion Iron, and Steel Company which, until a year or two ago was the only manufacturer of wire rods in this country could not dictate prices. The United States Steel Company at Pittsburgh enabled these independent concerns to get their wire rods at reasonable prices, and they could consequently make a profit in manufacturing the wire rods into the finished product. About four or five weeks ago a delegation representing these independent companies visited Ottawa and interviewed the Minister of Finance.
They presented their case, I understand, as thoroughly as they could; they stayed here some days, and they told the Minister of Finance that if he gave a bounty to the manufacturers of wire rods, or if he put a tariff on, which would practically have the same effect, he was placing power in the hands of these two companies, viz., the Dominion Iron and Steel Company and the Steel Corporation of Canada, by which they could put every independent wire manufacturing company in this country out of business. In the past, if the Dominion Iron and Steel Company or the Steel Corporation of Canada said to these independent concerns: You will have to pay a bigger price for your wire rods, all they had to do was to send their orders to Pittsburgh and get their raw material from the United States. But, the effect of this new arrangement is that these independent concerns are no longer able to import their rods from the United States. Even yet, under this tariff) some of them will have to import wire rods, made from Bessemer steel, for certain kinds of finished products, but in the main they will be compelled to purchase their wire rods from those two companies, which are the only manufacturers of wire rods in Canada.

This deputation, representing these interests, visited the Minister of Finance in this city, and they presented their case to him. Of course, the Minister of Finance has assured us that he will see to it that the smaller independent concerns get fair treatment and are not put out of business. That is all very fine, but I insist that, if his tariff proposals become law, he is putting every independent wire nail manufacturing company in this country in the hands of these t-wo concerns-and why? Both these companies, as I understand it, propose to go in for the manufacture of the finished products. What then will be the effect of this tariff? It will he, that these two companies can say to the independent concerns: you must pay so much for your raw material; and, if these two mergers want to go ultimately into the manufacture of the finished products of nails and wire, after raising the price of raw material to independent concerns they can drop the price of nails and wire, to such a point that they absolutely will compel every independent concern in this country to go out of business. Does the Minister of Finance deny that, untrammelled and unhindered by his influence or some other, that cannot, be done under this tariff proposal? The Minister of Finance does not answer. He may have the utmost faith in the good intentions of these two companies, but it is a very strange thing that the other manufacturing concerns who interviewed him do not possess the same confidence in them. I believe there was a proposal for an arrangement between these two concerns and the independent concerns, that if the tariff were to be put on they would not raise the price of the raw material, but my information is that an agreement was not reached on that point, and yet the Minister of Finance calmly asks u, to support this proposal. And Sir, so far as the consumer is concerned, the ultimate effect of the tariff is, that if these two great mergers put the independent concerns out of business, the consumer will have to pay the higher price in the end. I listened very carefully, and I have read carefully, what the Minister of Finance had to say on that subject, and while he did say something to the effect that he would see that no injustice was done, he did not say that if this proposal became law, these two companies would not enjoy the power I have mentioned. I make this protest here, because the matter has been brought to my attention by a large number of my own constituents.
In closing, I desire to say that I listened

with more or less surprise to certain statements that were made in this House by my hon. friend from Brandon (Mr. Aikins). That hon. gentleman, who, I am sorry is not in his place to-night, is not a very happy individual these days. He is, I believe, one of those who are not entirely pleased with the tariff proposals of the Minister of Finance. The hon. member for Brandon is a very loyal Conservative; he is what you would call a real good Tory at heart, and, not wishing to attack the Government of which he is a supporter, he turned his attention to an attack on the late Administration, and he gave us a review of the history of the West. I am not going to follow him in that review, except to say that the hon. member for Brandon has lived in the West for a great many years; he has seen the changes which took place in that country previous to 1896, and for the fifteen succeeding years, and it was a source of surprise to me . to hear him lay the blame at the door of the late Administration for the serious conditions which confront the people of the West to-day. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Aikins) is one of the respected citizens of Winnipeg, and I believe he has become wealthy in the practice of his profession. He has seen, under the Liberal Administration, his own city of Winnipeg develop from a place of very small dimensions until it is to-day the third city in this great Dominion. He has seen the West populated; he has seen the transportation systems grow throughout the length and breadth of that country. During the fifteen years of the Liberal Government he has seen two new provinces carved out of what years ago was trackless prairie. He has seen other changes, he has seen many things done in the interests of the farmers of the West by the Liberal Government, and finally the hon. gentleman owes his position in this House as a supporter of the Government, and not a supporter of an opposition, owing to the fact that the Liberal Administration went down to defeat in support of an issue that primarily had for its object the benefiting of the great masses of the people of this country, the farmers and consumers. He said we had done nothing and he reminded ns of what the present Government had done. I regret that among the things he took credit for was the reduction of the freight rates in western Canada by the decision of the Board of Railway Commissioners. If there is one body in this country that I would deplore seeing brought into the arena of partisan discussion, it is the Board of Railway Commissioners, be-

cause the moment that is done, in my judgment, the usefulness of that board is impaired. Surely the Government does not support the view taken by the hon. member for Brandon that any credit is due to it for that decision? My recollection of the documents in connection with that case is that shortly after the present Government came into power the Winnipeg Board of Trade instituted an inquiry or made a complaint to the Government and to the Board of Railway Commissioners. They took up that complaint, and, as I understand, by order of the Board of Railway Commissioners, this investigation was prosecuted. The provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta appointed a counsel to represent the people of the West before that commission. In the prosecution of the case no one took so active a part on behalf of the people of the West as did the counsel who was appointed to represent the two provinces. I am very much surprised that the hon. member for Brandon should be in such a bad case that in order to put something down to the credit of this Government he had to bring the Board of Railway Commissioners into partisan discussion.
I	have spoken somewhat longer than I had intended to and I have spoken because I feel the responsibility of expressing plainly, and as honestly as I can, the views of the people whom I represent in this House. I am free to say that the tariff proposals are a great disappointment to the people of western Canada. I suppose it is too late for a change or for any remedy, but I do wish that that open mind of the Minister of Finance would open for a little while on the other side and that
at least, when he brings down
II	p.m. another Budget Speech, it may
have more cheer, more hope, more promise in it for the future welfare and well-being of the people west of the Great Lakes than anything I can find in the proposal with which he so recently favoured us.

Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention to occupy very much of the time of the House at this late hour. I would like to compliment the hon. member for Humboldt (Mr. Neely) on his oration. I feel that he has, considering the length of the speech which he has delivered, done remarkably well. I sometimes feel that members from the western provinces take up a very great deal
of the time of this House, and at other times I feel as if the members from the Maritime provinces take up a great deal of time. It seems to me that the condition of affairs in the province of Ontario, is sometimes neglected by those of us who are responsible to the poeple there whom we represent. We do not occupy the time in debate that we should, and I feel that it is my duty representing a rural constituency, to make a few remarks upon this question.
I do not intend to try to answer the speech of the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat. I do not feel that I could answer that speech, and I feel satisfied that he has possibly done what he felt to be the best he could in the interests of the people he represents. I do not know whether, when he asked the question: What is meant by adequate protection? he expected to get a reply. I do not think it would be possible for any man to make a reply to the question as to what is adequate protection. But I would like to advise the hon. member for Humboldt and other hon. members on the opposite side of this House of the fact that the moment they swerved from the National Policy as it existed during the regime of the Conservative party and adopted the policy of free trade that they tried to present to us in 1911, they found out from the electors very decidedly what inadequate protection meant.
Coming, as I said, from a purely rural constituency, I feel that I must give expression to my opinion in connection with the tariff as it will affect our county when applied in accordance with the announcement contained in the Budget speech of my hon. friend the Finance Minister (Mr. White). I was somewhat surprised the other day to hear the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie)-and I am sorry he is not present this evening-when he spoke upon the reduction or abolition of duties on farm implements. He made the remark that he was sorry that some of his colleagues representing neighbouring ridings were not in their seats in order that they might give expression to their opinions. He undertook to state what the existing condition of affairs was in his riding. What he said can be seen in ' Hansard,' and therefore it is not necessary for me to read it, but his observations were to the effect that he had made inquiry and found from the electors of the agricultural portion of his constituency that they would be pleased

to have the duties removed from farm implements. I was not surprised. If any member of Parliament would go to the agricultural electors in his constituency and say to them: We are going to remove the duties from farm implements and we feel that you will get your implements cheaper, he would naturally get a reply to the effect indicated by the hon. gentleman if they thought they were going to save a little money. I have been going up and down at intervals since the session began, and when I arrived in my county I did not hear of any of the agriculturists there complaining about a money stringency or depression. After reading the speech of the hon. member for South Wellington, I felt that it was my duty, when I had gone home for the Easter holidays, to inquire into the state of affairs that existed. I started on this expedition of inquiry, and met farmers of North Wellington and of South Wellington. One farmer living close to the town in which I reside, when I asked him how he thought the new tariff was going to affect the farmers, said he was surprised at the criticism and that he thought the farmers had no reason to complain. He said: I brought into town two teams of farm horses for which I found a buyer at $1,200. That is equal to $300 per head for horses. Well, I feel that if the farmer can raise agricultural horses and take them into a neighbouring town and sell them at $300 a head-he has not much reason to complain. I got into conversation on the train, some time ago, with -a gentleman who is one of the best friends the hon. member for South Wellington (Mir. Guthrie) 'has. We were discussing the abolition of duty on cattle going into the United States. I knew he was a big stock dealer and .so I said: I suppose you will be selling a lot of cattle. He said: I have 103 head to sell. I said that would represent quite a sum of money, and he agreed that it would for he was to get 8 cents per pound. I said that he would receive great benefit by the removal of the duty from cattle going into the' United States, His answer was, ' Unfortunately, in the interest of my party, the 103 head of cattle for which I am receiving 8 cents a pound and which are to be shipped this week are not going to the United States but 'to Montreal.' They were not the quality of cattle which the people of the United States wanted from Canada and from which they had removed the duty. The United States

seem to know pretty well what they want; they wanted cattle which they could use for almost any purpose. The people of Canada made one of their greatest mistakes in reducing their stock of all kinds for what I feel was nothing more nor less than a bait. And when the time came that the people of the United States felt that they had enough of this cattle imported not only from Canada hut from the Argentine-because they had opened their m'aiket3 to others besides ourselves-they immediately applied the tuberculine test. They did not need to apply their test to Canadian cattle, but they applied it fox the same reason that they applied the test for diseased hogs when they felt that they had received enough of the Canadian product. When that was the position, they did what every Government should do-arrange so as to protect their own people first.
Last session I was surprised to hear a proposition laid down by the hon. member for South Wellington. That hon. gentleman and I are very good friends, and I have a great respect for him, for I feel that he is an able representative of one part of the county, a part of which I also represent. So, I am not saying anything in his absence that I would not say if he were present. Last session he spoke of the county of Wellington as being the greatest producing county in live stock. Of course it is a great producing county in live stock. He explained, and I believe he was conscientious about it, that in years gone by we had found in Buffalo a splendid market for our lambs, and that Buffalo was the natural market for lambs shipped from Wellington. On looking up the record of the markets of this country and the United States for the last three months, I find that many carloads of lambs had been shipped from Buffalo and other portions of the United States into Canada. And so the hon. gentleman's argument does not apply at this time. I find that the highest price paid for lambs in Buffalo on Saturday was $8.40, as compared with $9.85 paid in the city of Toronto. These are matters that affect directly the people of the county I represent, and such are the matters I deem it my duty to discuss.
I have been somewhat surprised that one of the members of the Opposition nas not offered an amendment in the course of this debate. We have been waiting to hear what their views are, and hoping to have an opportunity to speak on their

amendment. I feel it is just possible that they are not agreeing among themselves possibly as well as they would like to. It has always been the policy of the Liberal party when in Opposition in this House to advocate free trade. I do not think that any Liberal member who has been in the House for any length of time will deny that. In 1891, when the present leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) was in opposition, before he came into power, he was calling for 'free trade as they have it in England,' and for unrestricted reciprocity; and the Liberal party had the orators of Canada and the United States going from one part of this province to the other advocating what they thought was right at that time. But at the same time I felt that the leader of the Opposition of that day did not have any faith in it. However, after the Liberal party came into power in 1896 they did not make any such changes in the tariff as they are advocating in this House at the present time. Even their reciprocity agreement did not go as far the present Minister of Finance has gone in the reduction of duties on farm implements. I feel sure that we as representatives of the eastern portion of the Dominion of Canada can go to our people without any sins to answer for, and tell them that the hon. Minister of Finance has made-if they feel that it is a benefit- greater reductions in the duty on farm implements than the reciprocity agreement would have given them had it been put into effect in 1911.
Although some hon. gentlemen opposite have come out pointedly and in a straightforward manner for free trade-and I give the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark), my namesake, and the hon. member for Westmorland (Mr. Emmerson) credit for doing so-I think that if hon. gentlemen desire to advocate free trade in agricultural implements and in wheat, they should be men enough to stand up in a body and advocate free trade. Then, 'if they go to the polls on a free trade platform and come back victorious, we will see what effect it will have upon this country.
We have heard a great deal about the tax upon foodstuffs, which hon. gentlemen have denounced as being a very great burden upon the people. I have felt it my duty to endeavour to get information upon which I could come to the conclusion as to the effect of the duties on foodstuffs upon the high cost of living in Canada. In this connection I found the following article in the press the other day:
Speaking in support of their policy of ' free food,' opposition members are making much of the argument that it would lift the ' burden of food taxation, under which the people are groaning.' The contention looks good upon the surface, and no doubt makes an attractive appeal, but it will scarcely stand the test of a careful examination. Meats, poultry, eggs, fish, dairy products, and bread-stuffs, are the commodities which go to make up the dinner table of the average Canadian. The amount of customs duty collected from the import of these, last year, should form the fairest possible index of the extent to which our food is taxed. According to the latest available information in the reports of the Customs Department, the amount of duty collected on meats and poultry brought into Canada in 1913, totalled $1,040,547. Divide this among the population of the Dominion and it will be found that this * terrible taxation ' of meat, amounted in a year to the sum of thirteen cents per head -the cost of half a pound of steak.
The duty collected from the importation of eggs for 1913, amounted to $327,123. Divide it among eight million persons, and it amounts to a fraction more than four cents per head, or to the retail cost at present, of two eggs.
On fish last year the amount of duty collected was $361,116. Divide it among the population of the country and there is disclosed the tax of four cents per head.
Duty collected on imported bread-stuffs last year totalled $261,409. Divide it among eight million persons, and the * crushing burden ' amount to a fraction more than three cents per head.
It will, therefore, be seen that the total amount of duty collected on meats, poultry, eggs, fish, dairy products, and breadstuffs for the whole of 1913 amounted to under thirty cents per head of population, a sum which does not seem to much warrant the assertion that we are ' groaning ' under a * terrible food tax.'
The question of the reduction of the cost of living is one which a great many people have tried to explain, but to my mind those who have endeavoured to explain it are nearly as far away from a conclusion as they ever have been. I think it would be a benefit to us or to any people to get as closely allied with the consuming centres as possible. The improved means of transportation that we have are beneficial as far as the cost of living is concerned. I think the hon. member for Brandon was on the right track the other night when he said he believed that if the waterways of the West were properly developed an impetus would be given to the milling industry that would make it more than ever a world competitor. What applies to the West certainly applies to the East as well. The members of this House will remember that a few weeks ago a delegation of 2,000 persons came here from the province of Ontario. The members of this delegation were interested in trying to exact from this Government subsidies for hydro-radial railways



to be built in the province of Ontario. I am not in a position to say what conclusion the Government of the day has come to in that regard, but, as a resident of the province of Ontario, I feel that we are not too well supplied with railways. It may be a surprise to some of the people who are clamouring for transportation in the West to know that there are people living in the thickly-populated portions of our riding who are fifteen or twenty miles from the nearest railway station. These people have been highly taxed; they will sooner or later undertake the construction of hydroradial railways, and when these railways are constructed the people will be placed in communication with the great markets; the country will be built up under a policy of protection and the people will be induced to come back on the land.
There has been quite a decrease in the rural population of some of the western Ontario counties. Many of our people have gone out to our great West and we know and are delighted that they have prospered. But the people who are left here to till the soil in the old province of Ontario, those who came in in the earlier days a great many years ago, and had to endure many hardships are entitled to some consideration. I feel that if the Government, as I hope they will, see fit to give some help towards the construction of hydro-electric railways throughout that part of Ontario, and with or without aid these railways must come sooner or later, the farmers in the sections removed from the stations on the lines of the steam railways will be able to send their products in small quantities more rapidly into the splendid market centres in our manufacturing towns. They will then be in a better position than they are to-day even under the new tariff with the great reduction of 5 per cent on agricultural implements.
I shall not speak further to-night, as a further opportunity for discussion will be afforded during the debate on the amendment of the Opposition. I do wish to state, however, that I, as a humble follower of the present Administration, after making inquiry from the people in my county and in the surrounding counties, can assure the present Administration that they are giving what the people consider perfectly satisfactory government. I would like to compliment the Minister of Finance on the splendid Budget speech which he delivered, and at the same time to congratulate him on his restoration to health. I can assure him that the electors of North Wellington .are

satisfied that if he does not know exactly how to arrange the tariff in the interest of all the people in this country, he must have the credit of having made,- as he has done in every Budget speech since the Government came into power, an enlightened guess as to what would suit the people throughout the Dominion of Canada. After what he has done in the present Budget, I, as one of t e humble followers, will be pleased to go back to my constituency when the time comes and to pin my faith to the Minister of Finance-, as to the other members of the Government and our leader (Mr. Borden) who has endeared himself to the whole Dominion of Canada.
On motion of Mr. Sinclair, the debate was adjourned.
